title_original: Piknic : Deborah Turbeville In Upper Atmosphere
excerpt_original: In Seoul, piknic is presenting South Korea’s first monographic exhibition devoted to Deborah Turbeville (1932–2013), conceived in collaboration MUUS. Cet article Piknic : Deborah Turbeville In Upper Atmosphere est apparu en premier sur The Eye of Photography Magazine .

blocks.text: In Seoul, piknic is presenting South Korea’s first monographic exhibition devoted to Deborah Turbeville (1932–2013). Designed in collaboration with and based on the MUUS Collection, Deborah Turbeville: Atmosphere brings together nearly 200 works in a distinctly ethereal exhibition setting.

Born in Stoneham, Massachusetts, in 1932, Deborah Turbeville did not immediately begin her career as a fashion photographer. She initially worked as an editor at Harper’s Bazaar and Mademoiselle before turning to photography in the 1960s. By the following decade, her images had established a visual language that challenged advertising conventions while distinguishing her work from that of contemporaries such as Helmut Newton and Guy Bourdin. She favoured female figures in introspective, contemplative poses, sometimes seemingly disconnected from one another. Clothing, and therefore the product itself, became secondary, giving way to an enigmatic narrative.

Turbeville preferred to construct her images around an overall atmosphere, carefully staged through the use of Polaroids and numerous sketches. In compositions reflecting her fascination with ruins and the faded interiors of ballrooms and boudoirs, the exhibition at piknic demonstrates how her Bathhouse series (1975) represented a break with the visual conventions of the time, provoking outrage among some rather misogynistic observers.

Richard Grosbard, director of MUUS, recalled that her “grainy and faded” images shocked “some critics and readers, who imagined they saw themes such as heroin addiction and lesbianism.” Produced at the Asser Levy public baths in New York for Vogue , the series depicts five models in swimsuits occupying an enclosed space, apparently without interacting with one another. None looks towards the camera, or therefore at the viewer. Their poses sometimes appear languid, almost absent-minded, their gazes distant and disconnected.

This controversial series marked Turbeville’s emergence as a photographer. Her distinctive aesthetic was further developed in 1975 with the publication of Maquillage . Produced in an edition of 1,000 copies, it nevertheless approaches the form of an artist’s book, or at least a manifesto. Combining cut-up photographs, handwritten annotations and fragmented texts, it establishes a photographic practice in which images are scratched, torn and pinned together. Her Polaroids were likewise frequently altered, contributing to an aesthetic of erasure, or rather of atmosphere the central theme of the exhibition in which the presence of things is suggested rather than fully revealed.

In Seoul, the exhibition also highlights lesser-known aspects of her work, particularly her fascination with Russian urban settings and the landscapes of Mexico, where she owned a house. Her Studio St. Petersburg series (1997), for example, evokes the writings of Pushkin, Dostoevsky, Akhmatova and Brodsky, while also drawing on the cinema of Alain Resnais, Ingmar Bergman and Rainer Werner Fassbinder. Here, she places her figures in settings that are almost entirely dilapidated. She also photographed dancers from the Mariinsky Theatre, capturing the grace and evanescence of their movements in a celebration of fleeting moments, a sensibility equally characteristic of Turbeville’s work.

The rediscovery of Deborah Turbeville’s work owes much to the MUUS Collection. Founded by Michael W. Sonnenfeldt and specialising in the archives and works of twentieth-century American artists, MUUS acquired the Deborah Turbeville archive in August 2020. The collection includes more than 80,000 negatives, around thirty personal journals, research notebooks, Polaroids and manuscripts. Under the direction of Richard Grosbard, and with the involvement of photography historian Nathalie Herschdorfer and researcher Maeva Dubrez, a contributor to this publication, the photographer’s archives have since provided the basis for several exhibitions, notably the highly accomplished Photocollage at Photo Elysée.

The exhibition presented by piknic is no less remarkable. It offers an opportunity to consider Turbeville beyond her historical role in fashion photography. It demonstrates the extent to which her work was guided by a vision of photography founded on the alteration of images, the memory of places and the construction of indeterminate, atmospheric narratives, seeking as much to reveal as to conceal.
Deborah Turbeville: Atmosphere Piknic Du 23 octobre 2026 au 28 février 2027 30 Toegye-ro 6ga-gil, Jung District Seoul Corée du Sud
